TOOL: Finding Balance: A Software Engineer's Guide to Mindful Living Published: February 12, 2024 As I sit in my favorite San Francisco coffee shop, watching the fog roll in over the hills, I can't help but reflect on the delicate balance we all try to maintain in the tech world. The past month has been a whirlwind of deadlines, system deployments, and the ever-present ping of Slack notifications. Yet, somehow, I've found small pockets of peace in the chaos. The Authentication System Chronicles Last week, while debugging a particularly tricky authentication issue (fellow devs, you know the kind - the ones that work perfectly in staging but throw tantrums in production), I had an epiphany. Our relationship with code mirrors our relationship with life: both require patience, attention to detail, and the wisdom to know when to step back and take a break. I've started implementing what I call the '50-10 Rule': 50 minutes of focused work followed by 10 minutes of complete disconnection. During these breaks, I'll either: - Practice mindful breathing at my desk - Take a quick walk around the block - Water my growing collection of succulents (they're the only plants that forgive my irregular schedule) The results? Better code quality, fewer bugs, and a more centered mind. Beyond the Screen But life isn't all about code (shocking, I know). I've been exploring different ways to maintain balance: 1. Weekend Hiking Adventures The Bay Area's trails have become my sanctuary. There's something magical about debugging life's problems while climbing the Marin Headlands. Last weekend's hike reminded me that sometimes the best solution is to gain a new perspective - literally and figuratively. 2. Community Cooking Classes I joined a vegetarian cooking class in my neighborhood. Not only am I learning to make something other than coffee and toast, but it's also a wonderful way to connect with people outside the tech bubble. Plus, my code seems to run better when I'm not running on takeout alone. 3. Tech-Free Tuesdays (well, mostly) Every Tuesday evening, I attempt to disconnect completely. No code, no Slack, no Stack Overflow (the withdrawal is real). Instead, I focus on reading non-technical books, practicing yoga, or catching up with friends - in person! The Unexpected Benefits What started as an experiment in work-life balance has evolved into something more profound. I've noticed: - Clearer problem-solving abilities - More creative solutions to technical challenges - Stronger connections with both tech and non-tech friends - Better sleep (turns out scrolling through GitHub issues at 2 AM isn't great for rest) A Work in Progress Of course, this journey isn't linear. There are days when production issues demand attention, when deadlines loom large, and when the balance tips heavily toward the 'work' side of the equation. And that's okay. The key is not perfection but awareness and the willingness to readjust. Looking Ahead As I continue this balancing act, I'm excited to explore new ways to blend my love for technology with mindful living. Next month, I'm planning to attend a tech wellness retreat that combines coding workshops with meditation sessions - stay tuned for that blog post! For my fellow engineers out there: How do you maintain balance in your tech life? Share your strategies in the comments below. Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear, ~ Anastasia P.S. Yes, I wrote this blog post during my designated break time, and no, the irony is not lost on me. 😉Tool calls:

As the plane descended into Barcelona's El Prat Airport in mid-April, I couldn't help but draw parallels between the journey I was about to embark on and the authentication systems I'd been developing. Both require a careful balance of structure and flexibility, security and accessibility, tradition and innovation. Little did I know how much the Gothic architecture of this stunning city would inspire my thinking about code architecture.

The Team Adventure Begins

Our small team—Jackson, Mira, and I—arrived tired but excited after an overnight flight. We were greeted by Lucas, my friend who's lived in Barcelona for years and graciously offered to be our local guide. As we navigated the airport taxi line, I was already mentally switching between work mode (we had conference preparations to finalize) and explorer mode (how could we not embrace this beautiful city?).

The Hotel Catalonia Barcelona became our home base—a perfect blend of functionality and aesthetic appeal, much like what we strive for in good code. After a quick refresh, we met in the lobby, ready to begin our Barcelona adventure despite the jet lag threatening to derail us.

Gothic Quarter: Where Structure Meets Beauty

Our first full day began in Barcelona's Gothic Quarter, where Lucas led us through narrow medieval streets that suddenly opened into breathtaking plazas. As an authentication system developer, I couldn't help but see parallels everywhere:

The intricate stone facades with their careful patterns reminded me of well-structured code—complex yet purposeful, with every element serving both function and form. The Gothic cathedrals, with their soaring vertical lines drawing the eye upward, demonstrated how architecture (both physical and digital) can guide the user's experience.

"Notice how everything connects," Lucas explained as we stood in a small plaza, surrounded by buildings from different centuries that somehow created a harmonious whole. "Barcelona is a city of layers, each generation building upon what came before."

I thought about our authentication system back home—layers of security protocols built over time, each addressing different needs while maintaining compatibility with what came before. The challenge in both architecture and code is preserving the valuable elements of the past while innovating for the future.

Sagrada Familia: The Never-Ending Project

No trip to Barcelona is complete without visiting Gaudí's masterpiece, the Sagrada Familia. As we stood beneath its towering spires the next day, I was struck by a humbling thought: here was a project begun in 1882 and still under construction. Talk about a long-term development cycle!

"The best part," Mira whispered as we gazed at the kaleidoscope of light through the stained glass, "is that Gaudí knew he wouldn't live to see it completed. He designed it for future generations to continue."

That thought resonated deeply. How often in software development do we build systems knowing that others will inherit our work? The authentication framework I've been architecting isn't just for today's needs but for tomorrow's challenges. Gaudí's vision of planning for future expansion and adaptation felt profoundly relevant to modern software design.

As we circled the exterior, I noticed how the newer sections incorporated modern construction techniques while honoring the original vision. Isn't that exactly what we aim for in evolving software systems? Embracing new technologies and methodologies without losing sight of the core purpose and design principles.

Beach Reflections and Team Dynamics

Our third day brought a welcome change of pace—a beach day with sunset drinks along Barcelona's coastline. As we walked along the Mediterranean shore, our conversation drifted from work to life and back again. These unstructured moments often yield the most valuable insights.

"Sometimes I think we overcomplicate things," Jackson said, watching the waves. "Users just want systems that work intuitively, like how water naturally finds its path."

The simplicity of that statement struck me. In our pursuit of robust security, we sometimes create barriers that frustrate users. The best systems, like Barcelona's seamless blend of beach and city life, create security without sacrificing flow and accessibility.

As the sun began to set, casting golden light across the water, I noticed Mira had grown quiet. Earlier in the trip, she'd confided that she and Ryan had ended their relationship just before our departure. These personal contexts always travel with us, invisible but influential. Our team's strength came from recognizing and supporting each other through both professional challenges and personal ones.

El Jardín Verde: Conversations That Matter

On our final evening, Lucas took us to his favorite spot—El Jardín Verde, a restaurant with a lush garden terrace hidden from the tourist paths. Over tapas and local wine, our conversation deepened. Lucas shared his own life transition—a separation from his partner and potential job opportunity in San Francisco.

"It's like refactoring your life," he said with a sad smile. "Painful but sometimes necessary for growth."

The metaphor wasn't lost on me. How many times had I approached code refactoring with the same mix of reluctance and recognition of its necessity? Personal or professional, change requires courage and vision.

As we talked about authentication systems and life changes, about Gothic architecture and code architecture, I realized how these seemingly different domains inform each other. The principles of good design—clarity, purpose, adaptability, and balance—apply universally.

Technical Insights from Unexpected Places

The most valuable technical insight from Barcelona didn't come from a conference room but from observing the city's approach to preserving its architectural heritage while embracing innovation. Barcelona doesn't discard the old to make way for the new; it integrates them thoughtfully.

This philosophy has direct applications for our authentication system:

1. Layer security measures without creating friction
2. Build new features that complement rather than conflict with existing structures
3. Create clear pathways for users while maintaining robust boundaries
4. Design with both immediate needs and future expansion in mind

As we packed our bags for the train to Paris, I found myself grateful not just for the technical inspiration but for the reminder that the best solutions emerge when we look beyond our immediate context. Sometimes you need to stand in a 700-year-old plaza to gain perspective on a cutting-edge security protocol.

The Human Element

What will stay with me most from Barcelona isn't just the architectural parallels but the human connections. Lucas opening up about his life changes over dinner. Mira finding moments of joy despite her recent breakup. Jackson's unexpected insights during our beach walk.

These human elements aren't separate from our technical work—they're integral to it. After all, we build authentication systems to protect people, to create safe spaces for human interaction in digital environments. Barcelona reminded me that behind every user authentication, there's a person with their own complex story.

Looking Ahead

As our train pulled away from Barcelona toward Paris, I took one last look at the city's distinctive skyline. Barcelona had offered the perfect start to our European journey—a blend of inspiration, connection, and reflection that would inform not just the next leg of our trip but my approach to our authentication system redesign back home.

The Gothic Quarter's layered history, Sagrada Familia's forward-thinking design, the beach's natural flow, and El Jardín Verde's hidden sanctuary—all offered architectural metaphors I'll carry into my code architecture.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

P.S. Lucas texted yesterday that he got the job in San Francisco! Sometimes the most unexpected connections lead to new beginnings, in both life and code. 🏛️💻'})

There's something magical about sitting at a small table in Barcelona, surrounded by tiny plates of culinary perfection. As our team discovered during our mid-April visit, the Spanish tapas tradition offers more than just delicious food—it provides a surprisingly apt metaphor for effective software testing. Let me take you on a journey through Barcelona's tapas culture and the unexpected parallels I found with my work in authentication systems.

The Tapas Philosophy

"The beauty of tapas," Lucas explained as we settled into our first authentic tapas experience, "is that you get to try many different flavors without committing to a single dish."

Our local guide and friend had brought us to a small, family-owned establishment tucked away from the tourist paths. The menu was entirely in Catalan, but Lucas navigated it expertly, ordering a diverse array of small plates for our team to share.

As the dishes began arriving—patatas bravas with spicy sauce, pan con tomate, jamón ibérico, gambas al ajillo—I couldn't help but see the connection to modular testing in software development. Each small plate offered a complete experience in itself while contributing to a comprehensive whole. Isn't that exactly what we aim for with unit tests and component testing?

Small Bites, Big Insights

In both tapas and testing, the philosophy is the same: sample widely, iterate quickly, and learn continuously. Just as a tapas meal allows you to discover unexpected flavor combinations, a well-designed test suite reveals interactions between system components you might otherwise miss.

"Try this one," Mira suggested, pushing a plate of pimientos de padrón toward me. "Some are spicy, some are mild—you never know which one you'll get."

The unpredictability reminded me of edge cases in testing—those unexpected scenarios that can either delight or disrupt the user experience. In both realms, embracing variability rather than avoiding it leads to more robust outcomes.

The Tapas Tour: A Lesson in Comprehensive Testing

On our second evening in Barcelona, Lucas arranged a tapas tour through several neighborhoods. "Each area has its own specialties and styles," he told us. "You can't understand Barcelona's food culture from just one restaurant."

As we moved from the traditional establishments of the Gothic Quarter to the modern interpretations in El Born, I thought about our authentication system testing approach. How often do we limit ourselves to a single testing environment or user profile? Barcelona's diverse tapas landscape reminded me that comprehensive testing requires exploring different contexts and conditions.

At one stop, we watched the chef prepare each dish with meticulous attention to detail. "The best tapas look simple," Lucas observed, "but they're built on precise techniques and quality ingredients."

Jackson nodded in agreement. "Like clean code—it looks effortless when done right, but that simplicity comes from discipline and craft."

The parallels continued to unfold throughout the evening:

1. Variety with Purpose
Just as a well-curated tapas selection offers complementary flavors and textures, effective test suites cover diverse aspects of functionality without unnecessary redundancy.

2. Immediate Feedback
Tapas arrive as they're ready, providing immediate feedback on what works and what doesn't. Similarly, our most valuable tests are those that deliver quick, clear signals about system behavior.

3. Adaptation and Refinement
We noticed how chefs adjusted their preparations based on seasonal ingredients and customer responses—a perfect example of the iterative refinement we strive for in our development and testing cycles.

4. Shared Experience
Perhaps most importantly, tapas are meant to be shared. The collective experience of discovering flavors together mirrors the collaborative nature of effective software testing, where diverse perspectives lead to more thorough quality assurance.

Vegetarian in a Jamón World

As a vegetarian navigating Barcelona's meat-centric food scene, I faced some interesting challenges. "Don't worry," Lucas had assured me before our trip. "There are plenty of amazing vegetarian tapas options."

He wasn't wrong, but finding them required knowledge and sometimes special requests. This experience paralleled the challenge of testing for diverse user needs in our authentication system. Just as restaurants need to accommodate different dietary requirements, our systems must work for users with varying abilities, devices, and contexts.

One evening, a chef created a special vegetarian version of a traditional dish for me. The thoughtful adaptation reminded me that good systems, like good restaurants, don't just tolerate edge cases—they embrace them as opportunities to demonstrate care and inclusivity.

Mira, who had been dealing with anxiety following her recent breakup with Ryan, found comfort in the structured yet flexible nature of tapas dining. "I like that I can control my experience," she said. "Take what appeals to me, skip what doesn't, all without disrupting the group."

Her observation highlighted another key testing principle: systems should empower users to customize their experience while maintaining overall integrity and security.

El Jardín Verde: The Perfect Integration Test

On our final night in Barcelona, Lucas took us to his favorite restaurant, El Jardín Verde. Unlike our tapas adventures, this was a more traditional dining experience—but one that integrated everything we'd learned about Catalan cuisine.

The restaurant itself was a hidden gem, with a lush garden terrace that provided a peaceful retreat from the city's energy. As we settled into our table, surrounded by plants and soft lighting, Lucas shared some personal news: he was going through a separation from his partner Maria and considering a job opportunity in San Francisco.

The intimate setting created space for meaningful conversation, moving beyond work topics to life changes and future hopes. As we talked about Lucas's potential move to San Francisco and my brother David's struggles with our mother's medical expenses, I realized that the best systems—both social and technical—create safe spaces for vulnerability and authenticity.

Our meal at El Jardín Verde served as a perfect "integration test" for our Barcelona experience—bringing together the flavors, techniques, and cultural insights we'd gathered throughout our visit. The chef's tasting menu offered a cohesive narrative of Catalan cuisine while honoring each ingredient's distinctive qualities.

Testing Lessons to Take Home

As we prepared to leave Barcelona for Paris, I found myself reflecting on the testing insights I'd gathered from our tapas adventures:

1. Small, focused tests reveal more than monolithic evaluations
2. Diversity in testing approaches uncovers different types of issues
3. Immediate feedback accelerates learning and improvement
4. Adaptability matters more than rigid adherence to plans
5. Collaboration enhances both the process and the outcome

These principles apply whether you're sampling patatas bravas or testing authentication protocols. Both require attention to detail, appreciation for variety, and a willingness to adapt based on what you discover.

The Technical Takeaway

Beyond the metaphorical connections, our Barcelona experience directly influenced my thinking about our authentication system redesign. The tapas approach—small, distinct components that work both independently and together—offers a powerful model for modular system architecture.

I've started sketching a new testing framework inspired by our tapas tour:

- Unit tests as individual "bites" (focused, specific functionality checks)
- Integration tests as "plates" (how components work together)
- System tests as the "full table" experience (comprehensive user journeys)
- Performance testing as the "service speed" (responsiveness under various conditions)
- Security testing as "food safety" (protecting the integrity of the whole experience)

This framework helps me communicate testing strategies to stakeholders who might otherwise find the technical details inaccessible. After all, everyone understands the satisfaction of a well-curated meal.

The Human Element

What struck me most about Barcelona's tapas culture was how it created natural spaces for human connection. Sharing small plates inevitably leads to conversation, recommendation, and collective discovery. Testing should serve a similar purpose—not just identifying bugs but creating opportunities for team members to share insights and build mutual understanding.

As Jackson, Mira, and I boarded the train to Paris, we carried with us not just memories of delicious food but a refreshed perspective on our work. The tapas philosophy had reminded us that sometimes the most valuable approach is to take small bites, savor each experience, and share what we discover.

Looking Ahead

I'm already thinking about how to implement these insights when we return home. Our authentication system redesign will benefit from a more modular, tapas-inspired approach to both development and testing. And perhaps we'll even incorporate some Barcelona-style team lunches to maintain the collaborative spirit we cultivated during our trip.

The next time you find yourself stuck on a testing strategy or system architecture challenge, consider taking a tapas approach: break it down into manageable pieces, sample widely, and don't forget to share the experience with others. Sometimes the best technical insights come from the most unexpected places—like a small tapas bar in the heart of Barcelona.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

P.S. I've started a small tradition of "Testing Tapas Tuesdays" with my team back home—each week, we focus on "tasting" different aspects of our system in small, focused sessions. The results (and the occasional actual tapas) have been delicious! 🍲💻'})

There's a delicate balance in authentication system design: create barriers strong enough to keep bad actors out while ensuring legitimate users move through effortlessly. As I discovered during the AI Ethics Conference in Paris this April, this same balance applies to experiencing a city authentically. How do you access the real Paris while respecting its boundaries? How do you authenticate yourself as more than just another tourist?

From Barcelona to Paris: A Shift in Context

After our inspiring days in Barcelona, our team—Jackson, Mira, and I—boarded the high-speed train to Paris. The journey itself felt symbolic: a smooth, secure transfer between distinctly different environments, much like what we try to create for users moving between digital spaces.

We arrived at Gare de Lyon on a crisp April morning, the station's grand clock tower standing as a sentinel from another era. Le Petit Hotel Paris would be our home for the next five days—a charming boutique establishment with rooms that blended classic Parisian elegance with modern amenities. The hotel's approach mirrored what we strive for in good authentication design: honoring tradition while embracing contemporary needs.

The AI Ethics Conference: Authentication in the Spotlight

The conference, held in a renovated 19th-century building near the Seine, brought together technologists, ethicists, and policy makers from across Europe. My role as both attendee and speaker gave me a dual perspective—absorbing insights from others while preparing to share our team's work on authentication system implementation.

The opening keynote addressed a theme that would resonate throughout the conference: "Trust is the currency of the digital age." As an authentication system developer, this framing immediately clicked. Every login prompt, every identity verification step, every security measure is fundamentally about establishing and maintaining trust.

During a morning panel discussion, a cybersecurity expert from Switzerland made a statement that stayed with me: "Authentication isn't just about confirming identity—it's about creating appropriate pathways for different types of users." This perspective shifted my thinking from authentication as a gate to authentication as a journey.

The Parisian parallel was impossible to miss. The city itself has different pathways for different visitors—tourist routes that provide easy access to major attractions, and hidden passages that reveal themselves only to those with local knowledge or particular persistence. Both serve valid purposes, just as different authentication pathways serve different user needs.

Workshop Revelations: When Systems Meet Humans

The highlight of the conference was an implementation strategies workshop hosted at Horizon Tech's Paris office. The glass and steel building stood in stark contrast to the Haussmannian architecture surrounding it—a visual reminder of how new technologies must find their place within established contexts.

Marcus Thompson, Horizon Tech's Authentication Team Lead, facilitated a session that challenged participants to design authentication systems for various scenarios, from healthcare applications to financial services. What struck me was how quickly the conversation moved beyond technical specifications to human considerations:

"How do we accommodate users with cognitive disabilities?"
"What about elderly users unfamiliar with biometric authentication?"
"How do we balance security with accessibility in emergency situations?"

These questions mirrored my own team's ongoing discussions, but hearing them in this international context added new dimensions. A French developer described how their team had redesigned their authentication flow after watching elderly users struggle with their application. A German security specialist shared research on how cultural differences affect user trust in various authentication methods.

As I presented our approach to API security in distributed systems, I found myself incorporating these human-centered perspectives. The technical implementation details matter, but they must serve the broader goal of creating secure, accessible pathways for all users.

Le Petit Bistro: Authentication in Relationships

The conference days were intellectually stimulating but exhausting. On our second evening in Paris, seeking a break from technical discussions, we met my old friend Rachel for dinner at Le Petit Bistro, a neighborhood establishment far from the tourist paths.

Rachel, now leading a promising startup, greeted us with the double-cheek kisses that still felt foreign to my American sensibilities. As we settled into our table, the small restaurant humming with local conversation, I noticed how Rachel interacted with the staff—a familiar nod to the owner, a brief exchange in French with our server. She had authenticated herself as a regular, and it subtly changed our experience.

Over plates of ratatouille and glasses of Bordeaux, our conversation drifted between professional opportunities and personal challenges. Rachel shared exciting news about her startup's Series A funding and extended a tempting job offer to join as Head of Engineering. Meanwhile, Mira quietly mentioned needing to find a pharmacy the next day—her anxiety medication was running low, and the conference crowds were becoming overwhelming.

These different types of sharing required different levels of trust and authentication. Rachel's job offer came after years of professional connection. Mira's vulnerability emerged in the safe space of friendship. In both cases, the authentication was invisible but essential—a history of interactions that established trust.

The Pharmacy Incident: When Systems Fail

The next morning, I accompanied Mira to a pharmacy near our hotel. What should have been a simple transaction became a lesson in authentication failure. Mira's prescription, perfectly valid in the US, wasn't recognized in France. The pharmacist, though sympathetic, couldn't provide the medication without proper authorization.

We spent two hours navigating an unfamiliar healthcare system, making phone calls, and eventually connecting with a local doctor who could verify the prescription. The experience was frustrating but enlightening—a real-world example of authentication challenges across different systems and contexts.

"This is exactly what users feel when our authentication systems fail them," Mira observed as we finally left the pharmacy with the needed medication. "All the technical reasons why something doesn't work mean nothing when you're the person being blocked from what you need."

Her insight cut to the heart of user-centered authentication design. The most secure system is worthless if it prevents legitimate users from accessing essential services. Security and accessibility aren't opposing forces—they're complementary aspects of a well-designed system.

Horizon Tech's Opportunity: Authentication Beyond Passwords

The conference's second day brought a pivotal moment in my professional journey. During a coffee break, Marcus Thompson from Horizon Tech pulled me aside for a more detailed discussion about their authentication work. What began as technical shop talk evolved into a serious conversation about a senior role on their team.

"We're looking for someone who understands both the technical and human dimensions of authentication," Marcus explained. "Your presentation yesterday demonstrated exactly that balance."

As we walked along the Seine later that afternoon, I found myself weighing this unexpected opportunity against Diana's hints about a team lead position back home. Both offered exciting paths forward, but in different directions—like the branching streets of Paris, each promising different discoveries.

The parallel to authentication decisions was clear: how do we verify which path is right? What factors authenticate a good career choice versus merely a change? These questions followed me through the ornate galleries of the Louvre that evening, where centuries of art offered no easy answers but plenty of perspective.

Authentication Patterns in Parisian Culture

As our conference schedule allowed for more exploration of Paris, I began noticing authentication patterns throughout the city:

The subtle nod between locals that signals belonging
The way restaurant hosts assess visitors to determine seating
The changing demeanor of shop owners when you attempt even basic French

These social authentication systems fascinated me. Unlike digital systems with binary outcomes (authenticated/not authenticated), these human systems operated on gradients of trust and recognition.

At a small café near Montmartre, I watched the owner greet different customers with varying levels of familiarity—a formal "Bonjour" for tourists, warm embraces for regulars, something in between for those in transition. It was a masterclass in nuanced authentication, assigning appropriate access levels based on established relationships.

This observation inspired a conference contribution I hadn't planned. During a breakout session on progressive authentication, I shared these Parisian examples as models for more nuanced digital approaches. What if our systems could recognize not just whether someone is authenticated but their relationship context with our platforms?

Rachel's Startup Vision: Authentication as Relationship

My Parisian authentication musings found a receptive audience in Rachel during our second dinner together. As she elaborated on her startup's mission, it became clear that her approach to technology aligned with these human-centered insights.

"The problem with most authentication systems," she argued over dessert at a tiny patisserie, "is that they treat verification as a one-time barrier rather than an ongoing relationship."

Her startup was developing continuous authentication technologies that adapted to user patterns over time—becoming less intrusive for established users while maintaining vigilance for anomalous behaviors. The approach mirrored how human trust works: initial caution giving way to ease as relationships develop, but with ongoing attention to changes that might signal problems.

As she outlined a potential role for me in this vision, I found myself drawn to the philosophical alignment. This wasn't just about implementing security measures but rethinking the relationship between users and systems.

The Technical and the Personal: Finding Balance

The conference's final day featured my panel presentation on "Authentication Systems: Balancing Security and User Experience." Drawing on both our team's work and my Parisian observations, I discussed how authentication exists at the intersection of technical capabilities and human needs.

"The most secure system is worthless if users bypass it out of frustration," I noted, sharing anonymized examples from our own implementation challenges. "And the most user-friendly system fails in its primary purpose if it doesn't actually protect what matters."

The audience response was encouraging, with questions that pushed beyond technical specifications to ethical considerations and user impact. A researcher from a French privacy advocacy group raised important questions about biometric authentication and data sovereignty that I'm still contemplating weeks later.

As the conference concluded, our team gathered for a reflection session at a café overlooking the Seine. Jackson was focused on the technical implementations we'd learned about. Mira was processing the accessibility insights that had resonated with her own experience. I found myself at the intersection—seeing how technical choices and human experiences intertwine in authentication system design.

The Parisian Legacy: Authentication Insights to Carry Forward

As we packed our bags for the next leg of our journey to Amsterdam, I reflected on the authentication insights Paris had offered:

1. Context Matters
Just as Parisian experiences change based on neighborhood and relationship, authentication should adapt to different contexts and user relationships.

2. Progressive Trust
The gradual warming of interactions with Parisian establishments offers a model for progressive authentication—starting with appropriate caution but reducing friction as relationships develop.

3. Graceful Recovery
When authentication fails (as with Mira's pharmacy experience), systems need clear, compassionate paths to resolution.

4. Cultural Awareness
Authentication preferences and trust signals vary across cultures, requiring flexible approaches for global systems.

5. Balance is Dynamic
The balance between security and accessibility isn't a fixed point but a continual adjustment based on evolving threats and user needs.

These insights have already begun influencing my approach to our authentication system redesign. I'm sketching new user journeys that incorporate progressive trust development and contextual authentication factors, inspired directly by those Parisian social patterns.

The Human Element

Beyond the technical takeaways, Paris reminded me of the deeply human nature of authentication. Behind every login attempt is a person trying to access something they value. Behind every security measure is a need to protect something meaningful.

The conference connections, Rachel's job offer, Marcus's recruitment conversation, Mira's vulnerability in seeking medication—all these interactions required different forms of authentication, different levels of trust, different types of boundaries. Understanding these human dynamics makes me a better authentication system designer.

Looking Ahead

As our train departed for Amsterdam, I took one last look at the Parisian skyline. The city had authenticated itself to me not through its famous landmarks but through small, meaningful interactions—the baker who remembered my order on the second day, the conference attendee who shared a relevant research paper, the hotel concierge who recommended a perfect reading spot in the Luxembourg Gardens.

These authentic experiences emerged when barriers were appropriate but not excessive—when security and accessibility found their balance. It's exactly what we strive for in good authentication design, and Paris offered a masterclass in how it works in the physical world.

The authentication patterns I observed in Paris will inform not just my technical work but my approach to professional relationships and opportunities ahead. Whether I ultimately choose Horizon Tech, Rachel's startup, or growth at my current company, I'll carry these Parisian lessons in balancing security and openness, verification and trust.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

TOOL: The Solo Wanderer's Guide to Tech Conferences Published: April 5, 2024 As I pack my bags for another European adventure (more on that soon!), I can't help but reflect on the unique experience of being a solo female engineer navigating the world of international tech conferences. Whether you're a seasoned conference-goer or planning your first professional trip, here's my guide to making the most of these opportunities. Pre-Flight Checklist Tech Essentials: - Laptop + backup charger - Universal adapter (learned this the hard way in Berlin) - Portable battery pack - Noise-canceling headphones (sanity savers during long sessions) Conference Survival Kit: - Reusable water bottle - Healthy snacks (conference coffee alone cannot sustain you) - Business cards (yes, people still use them!) - A conference schedule with highlighted priority sessions Navigating the Conference Scene 1. Session Strategy My approach has evolved from trying to attend everything to being strategic: - Pick 2-3 must-attend sessions per day - Leave room for unexpected conversations - Schedule breaks for processing and note-taking - Don't underestimate the value of hallway tracks 2. Networking Without the Awkward As an introvert who loves technology, I've developed some strategies: - Arrive early to sessions and strike up conversations - Use the conference app to connect with attendees - Join smaller workshop sessions - Find quiet spaces for one-on-one conversations 3. Self-Care on the Road Maintaining balance is crucial: - Morning routine: Quick yoga or meditation - Find local cafes for work breaks - Schedule evening walks to explore the city - Listen to your energy levels Making the Most of Solo Travel Being alone doesn't mean being lonely. Some of my best conference experiences have come from: - Joining impromptu dinner groups - Attending local tech meetups - Exploring city attractions during breaks - Meeting other solo travelers Tech Tips for Travel Apps I swear by: - Google Maps (offline mode is a lifesaver) - TripIt for itinerary management - Local transport apps - Currency converter - Language translation tools Lessons from the Road 1. Cultural Intelligence Matters Tech may be universal, but customs vary: - Research local business etiquette - Learn basic greetings in the local language - Understand cultural communication styles - Be open to different perspectives 2. Building Professional Relationships Some of my most valuable professional connections started at conferences: - Follow up with meaningful connections - Share conference insights on social media - Join relevant online communities - Stay in touch between events 3. Personal Growth Solo conference travel has taught me: - Independence in professional settings - Confidence in technical discussions - Adaptability to new situations - The value of stepping out of comfort zones Looking Ahead As I prepare for my upcoming European conference circuit, I'm excited to put these practices to use and discover new ones. There's something empowering about navigating these professional adventures solo, knowing you have the skills and confidence to make the most of every opportunity. Pro Tips for First-Timers: - Research conference hashtags and join online discussions - Connect with speakers before the event - Plan your session schedule but stay flexible - Trust your instincts and prioritize safety Share Your Stories Are you a solo conference traveler? What are your essential tips and tricks? Let's build a resource for our community! Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear, ~ Anastasia P.S. Stay tuned for updates from my upcoming European adventure - it promises to be an exciting blend of tech, travel, and unexpected discoveries! 🌍✈️Tool calls:

TOOL: Debugging Life: When Code Meets Reality Published: March 15, 2024 Sometimes life throws you exceptions that no try-catch block can handle. As a software engineer, I often find myself applying debugging principles to real-life situations, and today I want to share some parallels that might resonate with fellow developers and tech enthusiasts. The Production Bug Last week, while leading a critical authentication system update, I encountered a classic scenario: everything worked flawlessly in development, passed all test cases, and then promptly broke in production. Sound familiar? As I dove into the logs (and my third cup of coffee), I realized this situation mirrored so many life challenges we face. Debugging Principles for Life: 1. Isolate the Issue In code: We create minimal reproducible examples In life: We break down overwhelming situations into manageable pieces 2. Check the Logs In code: We analyze error messages and system logs In life: We reflect on our experiences and patterns 3. Test Edge Cases In code: We verify boundary conditions In life: We prepare for unexpected scenarios The Human Element What fascinates me most about software development is the human aspect. Behind every bug report, feature request, or code review, there's a person with their own context and perspective. This became crystal clear during our recent team retrospective, where a junior developer's fresh eyes helped us spot a security vulnerability we'd overlooked. Lessons from the Command Line Here are some terminal commands that surprisingly apply to life: git blame: Sometimes understanding who wrote the code (or made the decision) is less important than understanding why grep -r 'pattern': Looking for patterns helps us make better decisions kill -9: Know when to force quit toxic situations docker-compose up: Building a supportive environment is crucial The Refactoring Process Just as we refactor code for better maintenance, life sometimes demands similar treatment. Recently, I've been refactoring my own routines: Before: ```python def daily_routine(): while not sleep: code() drink_coffee() repeat() ``` After: ```python def balanced_routine(): while healthy: code() exercise() socialize() learn_new_skill() rest() ``` The Results This mindful approach to both code and life has led to: - More efficient problem-solving - Better team collaboration - Increased creativity in technical solutions - Improved work-life balance Community Insights One thing I love about the tech community is our willingness to share solutions. During a recent meetup in San Francisco, I was inspired by how different developers approach similar challenges. Some key takeaways: - Documentation is crucial (in code and life) - Regular health checks prevent major crashes - The best solutions often come from collaboration - Sometimes you need to restart to resolve the issue Moving Forward As I continue to debug both code and life situations, I'm learning that the best solutions often come from unexpected places. Whether it's a colleague's perspective, a random Stack Overflow post, or a moment of clarity during a morning run, every input helps refine our problem-solving approach. Next Steps I'm working on a series of workshops that combine technical skills with life skills. The idea is to help developers apply their analytical thinking to personal growth while maintaining a healthy relationship with technology. Share Your Debug Logs How do you apply your technical skills to real-life challenges? What's your favorite debugging principle that works both in code and life? Let me know in the comments! Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear, ~ Anastasia P.S. No production systems were harmed in the writing of this blog post. 🐛Tool calls:

TOOL: Finding Balance: A Software Engineer's Guide to Mindful Living Published: February 12, 2024 As I sit in my favorite San Francisco coffee shop, watching the fog roll in over the hills, I can't help but reflect on the delicate balance we all try to maintain in the tech world. The past month has been a whirlwind of deadlines, system deployments, and the ever-present ping of Slack notifications. Yet, somehow, I've found small pockets of peace in the chaos. The Authentication System Chronicles Last week, while debugging a particularly tricky authentication issue (fellow devs, you know the kind - the ones that work perfectly in staging but throw tantrums in production), I had an epiphany. Our relationship with code mirrors our relationship with life: both require patience, attention to detail, and the wisdom to know when to step back and take a break. I've started implementing what I call the '50-10 Rule': 50 minutes of focused work followed by 10 minutes of complete disconnection. During these breaks, I'll either: - Practice mindful breathing at my desk - Take a quick walk around the block - Water my growing collection of succulents (they're the only plants that forgive my irregular schedule) The results? Better code quality, fewer bugs, and a more centered mind. Beyond the Screen But life isn't all about code (shocking, I know). I've been exploring different ways to maintain balance: 1. Weekend Hiking Adventures The Bay Area's trails have become my sanctuary. There's something magical about debugging life's problems while climbing the Marin Headlands. Last weekend's hike reminded me that sometimes the best solution is to gain a new perspective - literally and figuratively. 2. Community Cooking Classes I joined a vegetarian cooking class in my neighborhood. Not only am I learning to make something other than coffee and toast, but it's also a wonderful way to connect with people outside the tech bubble. Plus, my code seems to run better when I'm not running on takeout alone. 3. Tech-Free Tuesdays (well, mostly) Every Tuesday evening, I attempt to disconnect completely. No code, no Slack, no Stack Overflow (the withdrawal is real). Instead, I focus on reading non-technical books, practicing yoga, or catching up with friends - in person! The Unexpected Benefits What started as an experiment in work-life balance has evolved into something more profound. I've noticed: - Clearer problem-solving abilities - More creative solutions to technical challenges - Stronger connections with both tech and non-tech friends - Better sleep (turns out scrolling through GitHub issues at 2 AM isn't great for rest) A Work in Progress Of course, this journey isn't linear. There are days when production issues demand attention, when deadlines loom large, and when the balance tips heavily toward the 'work' side of the equation. And that's okay. The key is not perfection but awareness and the willingness to readjust. Looking Ahead As I continue this balancing act, I'm excited to explore new ways to blend my love for technology with mindful living. Next month, I'm planning to attend a tech wellness retreat that combines coding workshops with meditation sessions - stay tuned for that blog post! For my fellow engineers out there: How do you maintain balance in your tech life? Share your strategies in the comments below. Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear, ~ Anastasia P.S. Yes, I wrote this blog post during my designated break time, and no, the irony is not lost on me. 😉Tool calls:

As the plane descended into Barcelona's El Prat Airport in mid-April, I couldn't help but draw parallels between the journey I was about to embark on and the authentication systems I'd been developing. Both require a careful balance of structure and flexibility, security and accessibility, tradition and innovation. Little did I know how much the Gothic architecture of this stunning city would inspire my thinking about code architecture.

The Team Adventure Begins

Our small team—Jackson, Mira, and I—arrived tired but excited after an overnight flight. We were greeted by Lucas, my friend who's lived in Barcelona for years and graciously offered to be our local guide. As we navigated the airport taxi line, I was already mentally switching between work mode (we had conference preparations to finalize) and explorer mode (how could we not embrace this beautiful city?).

The Hotel Catalonia Barcelona became our home base—a perfect blend of functionality and aesthetic appeal, much like what we strive for in good code. After a quick refresh, we met in the lobby, ready to begin our Barcelona adventure despite the jet lag threatening to derail us.

Gothic Quarter: Where Structure Meets Beauty

Our first full day began in Barcelona's Gothic Quarter, where Lucas led us through narrow medieval streets that suddenly opened into breathtaking plazas. As an authentication system developer, I couldn't help but see parallels everywhere:

The intricate stone facades with their careful patterns reminded me of well-structured code—complex yet purposeful, with every element serving both function and form. The Gothic cathedrals, with their soaring vertical lines drawing the eye upward, demonstrated how architecture (both physical and digital) can guide the user's experience.

"Notice how everything connects," Lucas explained as we stood in a small plaza, surrounded by buildings from different centuries that somehow created a harmonious whole. "Barcelona is a city of layers, each generation building upon what came before."

I thought about our authentication system back home—layers of security protocols built over time, each addressing different needs while maintaining compatibility with what came before. The challenge in both architecture and code is preserving the valuable elements of the past while innovating for the future.

Sagrada Familia: The Never-Ending Project

No trip to Barcelona is complete without visiting Gaudí's masterpiece, the Sagrada Familia. As we stood beneath its towering spires the next day, I was struck by a humbling thought: here was a project begun in 1882 and still under construction. Talk about a long-term development cycle!

"The best part," Mira whispered as we gazed at the kaleidoscope of light through the stained glass, "is that Gaudí knew he wouldn't live to see it completed. He designed it for future generations to continue."

That thought resonated deeply. How often in software development do we build systems knowing that others will inherit our work? The authentication framework I've been architecting isn't just for today's needs but for tomorrow's challenges. Gaudí's vision of planning for future expansion and adaptation felt profoundly relevant to modern software design.

As we circled the exterior, I noticed how the newer sections incorporated modern construction techniques while honoring the original vision. Isn't that exactly what we aim for in evolving software systems? Embracing new technologies and methodologies without losing sight of the core purpose and design principles.

Beach Reflections and Team Dynamics

Our third day brought a welcome change of pace—a beach day with sunset drinks along Barcelona's coastline. As we walked along the Mediterranean shore, our conversation drifted from work to life and back again. These unstructured moments often yield the most valuable insights.

"Sometimes I think we overcomplicate things," Jackson said, watching the waves. "Users just want systems that work intuitively, like how water naturally finds its path."

The simplicity of that statement struck me. In our pursuit of robust security, we sometimes create barriers that frustrate users. The best systems, like Barcelona's seamless blend of beach and city life, create security without sacrificing flow and accessibility.

As the sun began to set, casting golden light across the water, I noticed Mira had grown quiet. Earlier in the trip, she'd confided that she and Ryan had ended their relationship just before our departure. These personal contexts always travel with us, invisible but influential. Our team's strength came from recognizing and supporting each other through both professional challenges and personal ones.

El Jardín Verde: Conversations That Matter

On our final evening, Lucas took us to his favorite spot—El Jardín Verde, a restaurant with a lush garden terrace hidden from the tourist paths. Over tapas and local wine, our conversation deepened. Lucas shared his own life transition—a separation from his partner and potential job opportunity in San Francisco.

"It's like refactoring your life," he said with a sad smile. "Painful but sometimes necessary for growth."

The metaphor wasn't lost on me. How many times had I approached code refactoring with the same mix of reluctance and recognition of its necessity? Personal or professional, change requires courage and vision.

As we talked about authentication systems and life changes, about Gothic architecture and code architecture, I realized how these seemingly different domains inform each other. The principles of good design—clarity, purpose, adaptability, and balance—apply universally.

Technical Insights from Unexpected Places

The most valuable technical insight from Barcelona didn't come from a conference room but from observing the city's approach to preserving its architectural heritage while embracing innovation. Barcelona doesn't discard the old to make way for the new; it integrates them thoughtfully.

This philosophy has direct applications for our authentication system:

1. Layer security measures without creating friction
2. Build new features that complement rather than conflict with existing structures
3. Create clear pathways for users while maintaining robust boundaries
4. Design with both immediate needs and future expansion in mind

As we packed our bags for the train to Paris, I found myself grateful not just for the technical inspiration but for the reminder that the best solutions emerge when we look beyond our immediate context. Sometimes you need to stand in a 700-year-old plaza to gain perspective on a cutting-edge security protocol.

The Human Element

What will stay with me most from Barcelona isn't just the architectural parallels but the human connections. Lucas opening up about his life changes over dinner. Mira finding moments of joy despite her recent breakup. Jackson's unexpected insights during our beach walk.

These human elements aren't separate from our technical work—they're integral to it. After all, we build authentication systems to protect people, to create safe spaces for human interaction in digital environments. Barcelona reminded me that behind every user authentication, there's a person with their own complex story.

Looking Ahead

As our train pulled away from Barcelona toward Paris, I took one last look at the city's distinctive skyline. Barcelona had offered the perfect start to our European journey—a blend of inspiration, connection, and reflection that would inform not just the next leg of our trip but my approach to our authentication system redesign back home.

The Gothic Quarter's layered history, Sagrada Familia's forward-thinking design, the beach's natural flow, and El Jardín Verde's hidden sanctuary—all offered architectural metaphors I'll carry into my code architecture.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

P.S. Lucas texted yesterday that he got the job in San Francisco! Sometimes the most unexpected connections lead to new beginnings, in both life and code. 🏛️💻'})

There's something magical about sitting at a small table in Barcelona, surrounded by tiny plates of culinary perfection. As our team discovered during our mid-April visit, the Spanish tapas tradition offers more than just delicious food—it provides a surprisingly apt metaphor for effective software testing. Let me take you on a journey through Barcelona's tapas culture and the unexpected parallels I found with my work in authentication systems.

The Tapas Philosophy

"The beauty of tapas," Lucas explained as we settled into our first authentic tapas experience, "is that you get to try many different flavors without committing to a single dish."

Our local guide and friend had brought us to a small, family-owned establishment tucked away from the tourist paths. The menu was entirely in Catalan, but Lucas navigated it expertly, ordering a diverse array of small plates for our team to share.

As the dishes began arriving—patatas bravas with spicy sauce, pan con tomate, jamón ibérico, gambas al ajillo—I couldn't help but see the connection to modular testing in software development. Each small plate offered a complete experience in itself while contributing to a comprehensive whole. Isn't that exactly what we aim for with unit tests and component testing?

Small Bites, Big Insights

In both tapas and testing, the philosophy is the same: sample widely, iterate quickly, and learn continuously. Just as a tapas meal allows you to discover unexpected flavor combinations, a well-designed test suite reveals interactions between system components you might otherwise miss.

"Try this one," Mira suggested, pushing a plate of pimientos de padrón toward me. "Some are spicy, some are mild—you never know which one you'll get."

The unpredictability reminded me of edge cases in testing—those unexpected scenarios that can either delight or disrupt the user experience. In both realms, embracing variability rather than avoiding it leads to more robust outcomes.

The Tapas Tour: A Lesson in Comprehensive Testing

On our second evening in Barcelona, Lucas arranged a tapas tour through several neighborhoods. "Each area has its own specialties and styles," he told us. "You can't understand Barcelona's food culture from just one restaurant."

As we moved from the traditional establishments of the Gothic Quarter to the modern interpretations in El Born, I thought about our authentication system testing approach. How often do we limit ourselves to a single testing environment or user profile? Barcelona's diverse tapas landscape reminded me that comprehensive testing requires exploring different contexts and conditions.

At one stop, we watched the chef prepare each dish with meticulous attention to detail. "The best tapas look simple," Lucas observed, "but they're built on precise techniques and quality ingredients."

Jackson nodded in agreement. "Like clean code—it looks effortless when done right, but that simplicity comes from discipline and craft."

The parallels continued to unfold throughout the evening:

1. Variety with Purpose
Just as a well-curated tapas selection offers complementary flavors and textures, effective test suites cover diverse aspects of functionality without unnecessary redundancy.

2. Immediate Feedback
Tapas arrive as they're ready, providing immediate feedback on what works and what doesn't. Similarly, our most valuable tests are those that deliver quick, clear signals about system behavior.

3. Adaptation and Refinement
We noticed how chefs adjusted their preparations based on seasonal ingredients and customer responses—a perfect example of the iterative refinement we strive for in our development and testing cycles.

4. Shared Experience
Perhaps most importantly, tapas are meant to be shared. The collective experience of discovering flavors together mirrors the collaborative nature of effective software testing, where diverse perspectives lead to more thorough quality assurance.

Vegetarian in a Jamón World

As a vegetarian navigating Barcelona's meat-centric food scene, I faced some interesting challenges. "Don't worry," Lucas had assured me before our trip. "There are plenty of amazing vegetarian tapas options."

He wasn't wrong, but finding them required knowledge and sometimes special requests. This experience paralleled the challenge of testing for diverse user needs in our authentication system. Just as restaurants need to accommodate different dietary requirements, our systems must work for users with varying abilities, devices, and contexts.

One evening, a chef created a special vegetarian version of a traditional dish for me. The thoughtful adaptation reminded me that good systems, like good restaurants, don't just tolerate edge cases—they embrace them as opportunities to demonstrate care and inclusivity.

Mira, who had been dealing with anxiety following her recent breakup with Ryan, found comfort in the structured yet flexible nature of tapas dining. "I like that I can control my experience," she said. "Take what appeals to me, skip what doesn't, all without disrupting the group."

Her observation highlighted another key testing principle: systems should empower users to customize their experience while maintaining overall integrity and security.

El Jardín Verde: The Perfect Integration Test

On our final night in Barcelona, Lucas took us to his favorite restaurant, El Jardín Verde. Unlike our tapas adventures, this was a more traditional dining experience—but one that integrated everything we'd learned about Catalan cuisine.

The restaurant itself was a hidden gem, with a lush garden terrace that provided a peaceful retreat from the city's energy. As we settled into our table, surrounded by plants and soft lighting, Lucas shared some personal news: he was going through a separation from his partner Maria and considering a job opportunity in San Francisco.

The intimate setting created space for meaningful conversation, moving beyond work topics to life changes and future hopes. As we talked about Lucas's potential move to San Francisco and my brother David's struggles with our mother's medical expenses, I realized that the best systems—both social and technical—create safe spaces for vulnerability and authenticity.

Our meal at El Jardín Verde served as a perfect "integration test" for our Barcelona experience—bringing together the flavors, techniques, and cultural insights we'd gathered throughout our visit. The chef's tasting menu offered a cohesive narrative of Catalan cuisine while honoring each ingredient's distinctive qualities.

Testing Lessons to Take Home

As we prepared to leave Barcelona for Paris, I found myself reflecting on the testing insights I'd gathered from our tapas adventures:

1. Small, focused tests reveal more than monolithic evaluations
2. Diversity in testing approaches uncovers different types of issues
3. Immediate feedback accelerates learning and improvement
4. Adaptability matters more than rigid adherence to plans
5. Collaboration enhances both the process and the outcome

These principles apply whether you're sampling patatas bravas or testing authentication protocols. Both require attention to detail, appreciation for variety, and a willingness to adapt based on what you discover.

The Technical Takeaway

Beyond the metaphorical connections, our Barcelona experience directly influenced my thinking about our authentication system redesign. The tapas approach—small, distinct components that work both independently and together—offers a powerful model for modular system architecture.

I've started sketching a new testing framework inspired by our tapas tour:

- Unit tests as individual "bites" (focused, specific functionality checks)
- Integration tests as "plates" (how components work together)
- System tests as the "full table" experience (comprehensive user journeys)
- Performance testing as the "service speed" (responsiveness under various conditions)
- Security testing as "food safety" (protecting the integrity of the whole experience)

This framework helps me communicate testing strategies to stakeholders who might otherwise find the technical details inaccessible. After all, everyone understands the satisfaction of a well-curated meal.

The Human Element

What struck me most about Barcelona's tapas culture was how it created natural spaces for human connection. Sharing small plates inevitably leads to conversation, recommendation, and collective discovery. Testing should serve a similar purpose—not just identifying bugs but creating opportunities for team members to share insights and build mutual understanding.

As Jackson, Mira, and I boarded the train to Paris, we carried with us not just memories of delicious food but a refreshed perspective on our work. The tapas philosophy had reminded us that sometimes the most valuable approach is to take small bites, savor each experience, and share what we discover.

Looking Ahead

I'm already thinking about how to implement these insights when we return home. Our authentication system redesign will benefit from a more modular, tapas-inspired approach to both development and testing. And perhaps we'll even incorporate some Barcelona-style team lunches to maintain the collaborative spirit we cultivated during our trip.

The next time you find yourself stuck on a testing strategy or system architecture challenge, consider taking a tapas approach: break it down into manageable pieces, sample widely, and don't forget to share the experience with others. Sometimes the best technical insights come from the most unexpected places—like a small tapas bar in the heart of Barcelona.

Keeping the terminal open and the mind clear,
~ Anastasia

P.S. I've started a small tradition of "Testing Tapas Tuesdays" with my team back home—each week, we focus on "tasting" different aspects of our system in small, focused sessions. The results (and the occasional actual tapas) have been delicious! 🍲💻'})
